tagline: Through Darien and down onto the old rice coast.
intro: The byway starts at the Sapelo Island Visitors Center and follows SR 99 into Darien, then US 17 past the Altamaha River plantations to the Needwood Church and School, 17 miles through McIntosh and Glynn counties with sweeping marsh views and live oaks draped in Spanish moss.

Darien was New Inverness when Highland Scots settled it in 1736, and in 1739 its leading men signed the first petition against bringing slavery into Georgia. Slavery came anyway in 1749, and the rice plantations along the river were worked by enslaved people.

moments.title: Fort King George
moments.text: A blockhouse rebuilt from old records and drawings stands at the oldest English fort remaining on Georgia's coast, the southernmost outpost of the British Empire in North America from 1721 to 1727.

moments.title: Butler Island
moments.text: Fanny Kemble came to this rice plantation in 1838 having been told the enslaved people were well treated, found otherwise, and kept a journal that some think helped turn Britain against the Confederacy.

moments.title: Hofwyl-Broadfield Plantation
moments.text: Rice grew in these marshes until 1913, then the Dent siblings started a dairy rather than sell the family home, and the marsh has since taken the rice fields back.
